# The Comeback That Won't Be Allowed: Vinesh Phogat vs India's Wrestling Establishment

## Barred from competition by the WFI despite international clearance, India's most famous wrestler faces a kafkaesque battle to salvage her Asian Games dream

Vinesh Phogat arrived at the National Open Ranking Tournament in Gonda, Uttar Pradesh, in May 2026 ready to wrestle. She had trained for months. She had, by her account, received clearance from the International Testing Agency and the World Anti-Doping Agency to compete from January 1, 2026. She had publicly declared her return from retirement. None of it mattered.

The Wrestling Federation of India barred her from entering. A 15-page show cause notice, citing anti-doping violations and indiscipline dating back to the 2023 national trials, had placed her under suspension until June 26, 2026. Vinesh was turned away at the door.

**A bureaucratic wall**

The WFI's case against Vinesh rests on allegations that she violated procedural rules during the 2023 trials — a period when Indian wrestling was already engulfed in crisis over sexual harassment allegations against then-president Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh. Vinesh was among the most prominent wrestlers who led public protests at Jantar Mantar, demanding accountability from the federation and the Indian government.

The current WFI administration, led by president Sanjay Singh, insists the suspension is a matter of rules enforcement, not retaliation. "No wrestler will get any special favour," Singh told reporters. The federation points to what it calls an incomplete response from Vinesh to disciplinary charges.

Vinesh's camp sees it differently. Her legal team maintains that the ITA and WADA clearances supersede any domestic federation ban. The dispute places India's wrestling body in open conflict with the international anti-doping framework — an uncomfortable position for a federation that depends on the United World Wrestling's recognition to function.

UWW, the global governing body, has so far declined to intervene, effectively backing WFI's authority over domestic competitions. It is a stance that has infuriated Vinesh's supporters but reflects the general reluctance of international federations to override national bodies on procedural matters.

**Paris and its aftermath**

The Gonda standoff cannot be understood without the context of Paris 2024. Vinesh's Olympic campaign was one of the most dramatic — and devastating — in Indian sporting history. She fought her way to the 50kg wrestling final, defeating world and Olympic champions en route, only to be disqualified on the morning of the gold medal bout for weighing 100 grams over the limit.

The disqualification, which denied her even a silver medal, prompted an outpouring of grief and rage across India. Vinesh announced her retirement from the sport shortly after, saying she could no longer carry the emotional weight.

Her decision to return in 2026, driven by a desire to compete at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, was widely celebrated. "If I give up, I won't be able to look at myself in the mirror," she said in a recent interview. The quote captured both her defiance and vulnerability — qualities that have made her a deeply resonant figure in Indian sport.

**A familiar pattern**

The WFI's treatment of Vinesh fits a broader pattern that has dogged Indian sports governance for decades. Athletes who challenge the system — whether through protest, legal action, or simply by demanding transparency — often find themselves frozen out through bureaucratic mechanisms. The federation's show cause notice, whatever its legal merits, arrives with suspicious timing: just as Vinesh attempts to qualify for a major international event.

Sakshi Malik, Vinesh's fellow wrestler and fellow protestor from the 2023 agitation, has urged Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya to intervene. The government has thus far remained silent — a familiar posture when sporting federations are involved.

**The diaspora's investment**

For the Indian diaspora, Vinesh Phogat is not merely an athlete but a symbol. During the Paris Olympics, NRI communities across the United States, Britain, and Canada organised watch parties for her bouts. When the disqualification was announced, diaspora-led petitions on Change.org gathered hundreds of thousands of signatures demanding a CAS review. Indian-American and British-Indian social media accounts drove the #JusticeForVinesh hashtag to global trending.

The connection runs deeper than sporting fandom. Vinesh's story — a woman from rural Haryana challenging entrenched patriarchal power structures in Indian sport — resonates powerfully with diaspora communities that often grapple with questions of Indian identity, gender equity, and institutional accountability from afar. Her treatment by the WFI reinforces a narrative that many NRIs find both infuriating and depressingly familiar: that in Indian sport, the system will always protect itself before it protects its athletes.

**What happens now**

The clock is ticking. The National Open Ranking Tournament in Gonda serves as a qualifier for the Asian Games. If Vinesh cannot compete by the time her suspension notionally expires on June 26, the window for qualification may have already closed.

Legal challenges are expected. Vinesh's team is exploring options before the Delhi High Court and potentially the Court of Arbitration for Sport. But the bureaucratic machinery moves slowly, and the Asian Games will not wait.

Vinesh Phogat has beaten world champions on the mat. Whether she can beat the Wrestling Federation of India in a boardroom remains an altogether different contest.
